body: I'm not sure I understand, if you have `<input autocomplete=username>` the user agent could populate the field with the end user's username. If you have `<input autocomplete=language>` the user agent could populate the field with the end user's language. When the user agent does the latter, it has to use BCP47 codes to encode the language. So for you, it might suggest to submit `en-US`, for me, it might suggest `nl`.

Hi @annevk, I understand what you wrote, but how does the user-agent know to insert en-US (when in actual fact, now that I have moved back to Canada, it should now be en-CA)?

Answer, it doesn't - it only knows what to insert in an input tagged with 'language' (@autocomplete="language") **based upon what I  (as end user) have previously provided as an answer.** 

If I have stored the value "Klingon" into my user-agent as my 'language', then per the spec, any time the user-agent finds an input tagged 'language' it would autofill the field with the response 'Klingon' based on the hint (ref: _"... for example prefilling the user's address **based on earlier user input**.  ...used to **hint to the user agent** how to..."_)

In this regard it is no different than knowing which email address to input in to an input tagged @autocomplete="email" (i.e., it doesn't know anything about any of my email addresses until I provide that information, at which point most browsers today ask if I want the browser to 'remember' that value) or for that matter gender (ref: autocomplete="sex") - and I argue that because it is storing data furnished by the end user, it is an unrealistic ask that individual users MUST initially furnish the correct language code in each individual user's browser 'preferences' (i.e. the 'lookup' table used to autofill tagged form inputs). 

Evidence: On my Chrome browser I have actually stored 2 different email values, and when presented with an input tagged @autocomplete="email", I am queried as to which email address to use. Presumably if browsers today also stored language field responses, individual users who speak/use more than one language could 'store' multiple options on their user-agent. (English, French, Klingon)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1228403/112029598-ce7cfc80-8b0f-11eb-92c1-1319c7bb074b.png)
[_alt: screen capture from Chrome browser showing where/how to store autocomplete values furnished by the end user_]

Editing the fields:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1228403/112031627-ece3f780-8b11-11eb-9b2e-d82fbb493b9e.png)
[_alt: screen capture from Chrome browser showing the ability to store 'answers' to @autocomplete values_]

I believe that the higher-order function here is being lost: the intention of this attribute and corresponding 'lookup table of values' (stored on each user-agent) was to allow users to fill out forms with common data (aka text strings) more quickly, and not to have an impact on the formulation or manipulation of the values furnished by the end user (i.e. form processing) which mandating a specific language code here is doing. If I want to make my 'language' Klingon, I should not be disallowed to do this (while also noting there is no ISO639-1 code for Klingon).

Klingon Ref: https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klingon_language#:~:text=The%20Klingon%20language%20(%20tlhIngan%20Hol,enough%20to%20talk%20in%20it.

> while also noting there is no ISO639-1 code for Klingon

There is, however, an ISO 639-2 code for Klingon: [tlh](https://iso639-3.sil.org/code/tlh).

@Yay295 sure, but that misses the point: most users will not know what an ISO639-1 or 639-2 code is... they know what their 'language' is, and that is what they will input into the text field - which according to the spec user-agents will then "remember" for next time (which is the practical application of what supported @autocomplete values does today: the browser asks me if I want for it to remember those values for next time).

I would expect something like
```html
<select name=language autocomplete=language>
  <option value=nl>Dutch
  <option value=en-US>American English
  <option value=tlh>Klingon
</select>
```

So you are saying that the *ONLY* way to use @autocomplete="language" is on a select element? If that is the case, it should be documented as such in the spec, as it is atypical of how that attribute is used - for example, it cannot be used on radio buttons or checkboxes (or any grouping element/mechanism).

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1228403/112145853-3fc0bc00-8bb1-11eb-9b14-b4b0b8402907.png)

Additionally, if providing the language code is ***required***, then a form input with that attribute and value, but lacking the language code, **SHOULD NOT** validate today (but it does). (@sideshowbarker ?)

So somewhere there seems to be a gap, and editorially, I find it quite restrictive on the page author to force usage of a select element here as the *ONLY* way of using the @autocomplete attribute for the value of language. However, if that is the case, it should be better documented in the spec.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1228403/112146734-4e5ba300-8bb2-11eb-95e9-94590f999a57.png)
I don't see why a radio button or checkbox wouldn't work either?

> I don't see why a radio button or checkbox wouldn't work either?

Hi Anne,

Because the spec says it can't:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1228403/112149681-9fb96180-8bb5-11eb-9adf-098bdd8b488c.png)

I'm also troubled by the lack of real logic here:

**Assertions:** 

- the @autocomplete attribute is to provide a "hint" to machines on how to fill in form fields 
- the @autocomplete attribute is NOT used for any type of form processing or error validation
- browsers today support a limited number of all of the values noted in the spec, and provide the 'hint' functionality as suggested (@autocomplete="language" does not appear to have any native browser support today)

**Use Case:**

- Client wishes to collect user information as a db table of text strings in natural (localized) language, including language information about the user. 
- The client has no use or need for collecting the language code string - there is no entry in the db for that data.
- A global company, the client anticipates multiple language values **of their users** (including languages that the website content currently is not translated to - but may nonetheless be the users native language: eg lang="oji" (Ojibwa)).
- The client **does NOT want** (due to design considerations) to use a select with all possible language code values (far in excess of 300 possible values - I stopped counting - but that would be a mighty large select...) 
[source: [https://www.loc.gov/standards/iso639-2/php/code_list.php](https://www.loc.gov/standards/iso639-2/php/code_list.php)]
- Per the ISO639-2 spec, there are language codes that would likely 'break' any functionality/usefulness when specified or captured as part of the form submission:
>- mis, for "uncoded languages";
>- mul, for "multiple languages";
>- qaa-qtz, a range reserved for local use.
>- und, for "undetermined";
>- zxx, for "no linguistic content; not applicable";

Given the above assertions, *WHY* are we mandating the usage of a language code on a form input? 
If the end client has no use for that data-string, why is it being added to the form? 
Will the addition of a language code on a form input affect browser behavior in any way? What value is this adding?

That does seem like an oversight indeed. Especially as elsewhere it suggests using radio buttons or checkboxes for languages. It seems "Text" was added in 723263410c0ceb5181ca684ea90d5034114462dd and nobody noticed until now that it's incorrect.

I'm not sure why language was originally added. If there are no implementations we could remove it I suppose.

> I'm not sure why language was originally added. If there are no implementations we could remove it I suppose.

That would be a regrettable choice, although the AG WG at W3C anticipated that the WHAT WG spec might remove some of the current values. It was for that reason that the 'values' were also [added to the WCAG 2.1 specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#input-purposes) in support of [Success Criteria 1.3.5](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#identify-input-purpose). Additionally, the emergent Personalization Module 1 is also leveraging those terms (taxonomy) for the proposed [@purpose attribute](https://w3c.github.io/personalization-semantics/content/index.html#purpose-explanation).

This issue came up due to a cross-functional review from the good folks at i18n, [who wanted the same request](https://github.com/w3c/personalization-semantics/issues/175) - adding the language code to the input. I continue to question why, as essentially the values of @autocomplete (and likewise our proposed @purpose) are metadata, and not part of the text output to the screen. Form inputs collect strings of data: interpreting those strings happens elsewhere in the stack/process. 

**This attribute simply provides a machine-readable hint for the input!**

I would prefer to see the following:
- Expand @autocomplete to also be valid on 'grouping' mechanisms (fieldset, [role="group"](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.1/#grouphttps://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.1/#group)) to address radiobuttons and checkboxes support.
```
 <fieldset autocomplete="language">
   <legend>What is your language?</legend>
    <label for="1">English</label> <input type="checkbox" id="1" value="English">
    <label for="2">Dutch</label> <input type="checkbox" id="2" value="Dutch">
    <label for="3">Klingon</label> <input type="checkbox" id="3" value="Klingon">
</fieldset>
```

- Remove the requirement for adding a language code to the metadata term "language", as it is not required for the 'hinting' purpose of @autocomplete and provides no specific functionality nor addresses any specific need that I can determine.
- **Encourage browser vendors to [support more values than they currently do](https://www.w3.org/WAI/GL/wiki/WCAG_2.1_Implementations/JF/research)** :-) (Last Updated Feb. 2018)

Well, the reason to require it to be a language code is mostly aimed at websites, to ensure all websites can handle the same filled in values. Otherwise my browser might associate "Nederlands" with language and use that on another site that wanted "nl" or "Dutch"; removing that uniformity would make it rather useless I think.

That completely depends on the form owner and the reason why they are collecting that data string. 

Some sites MAY need the language code in a specific format, others may be far less demanding (i.e. some sites MAY require 'nl', others might be happy to accept "Nederlands" "The Netherlands" "Holland"...) - the point is, nobody but the form author really knows how critical a value format is (likewise I've seen forms that *INSIST* on splitting up data like telephone numbers: 3 + 3 + 4 versus 10 characters per input), so respectfully I find that a weak argument.

*Forcing* form authors to do this would be overly prescriptive. If the form author NEEDS a specific format, use radio buttons or select options: if they are less fussy the form author should be able to use input type of text.

At the end of the day, I believe that the internationalization folks sort of missed the point here: **this is metadata** that furnishes a hint, and nothing more. Insisting on adding data formatting requirements here reduces the overall functionality and usefulness IMHO (and, because of the confusion and impracticality of this as currently written, is likely a reason why there is zero support for this attribute value today).

Given the current lack of robust support, it is an opportune time to fix this misinterpretation of the functionality of this attribute.

How could a user agent reasonably autofill across a wide variety of sites if they all used different value spaces for the same types? I guess you could argue it's bound to the site, but then what point is autofilling it? The site might as well remember it.

Hi Anne,

> How could a user agent reasonably autofill across a wide variety of sites if they all used different value spaces for the same types?

Based on the data furnished by the end user - in exactly the same way sites can autofill email addresses, or credit card numbers today: **it's whatever *you as a user* has stored on your user-agent.** 

If, in *YOUR* user profile (a simple lookup table with term:value) then that is what will be autofilled in a form. If you get the formatting wrong, it is up to the form validation to catch that error and provide the error message. So, if you store on your user-agent that your language is 'Dutch', then *every* form you encounter that asks for that value will be auto-populated (rather the browser will offer to auto-populate) with "Dutch". (Equally, if you stored the value "Pig Latin" in your profile, then every form seeking language that is tagged with @autocomplete="language" will fill in the input with Pig Latin - not because it is an official language, or because of an ISO language code, but rather because you stored that value on your machine. The language code is a red herring in this context - a distraction.)

If that is not what the format that the owner of a specific form needs or wants, they need to tell you (because otherwise, if you didn't have that value previously stored, and you were asked your language preference for the first time with no other 'formatting' requirements, you'd likely type in Dutch, or Pig Latin anyway... most users would probably not think to start with an arcane ISO language code - only geeks like us would even think that way ;-) )

Remember, the point here is to provide *A HINT*, not magically resolve all form issues. Again, if the form owner requires specific formatting, they can either enforce that through the form design (use a select, or if added, the grouping mechanism with radio buttons or checkboxes), and/or specifically request data in the format they require. We've all seen loads of websites that ask for your phone number with no spaces, yet other sites ask for "with spaces" or with "hyphenated" numbers. 

@autocomplete today cannot solve that issue either: @autocomplete's reserved values (tokens) are simply metadata - the tokens represent a taxonomy (which is why those values-as-metadata have been repurposed in WCAG 2.1). Yet only one taxonomy term is further insisting on associating a language marker to it, but nobody has shown why this is necessary, as it still likely doesn't have any bearing on the data-strings the form owner may NEED - it may be additional data that is discarded by the db design.

So this is not about which values are provided to specific form inputs, it's about tagging the inputs to ensure unambiguous 'responses' to unambiguous 'requests'

I agree there is a problem here, but I think the solution that makes sense is along the lines @annevk is implying - the value is a machine-readable one, and so should be matched to a machine-readable enumeration (e.g. a select, checkbox or button) which would require a change to the spec - and a demonstration that it works in practice or a commitment that it will.

The problem with expecting the browser to keep a set of user-generated strings in this case is as @annevk notes: You create a very large matrix of possible values for developers to have to deal with, and the likelihood of developers not managing to anticipate the full set of replies in cases where this is relevant would be somewhere very close to 100%.

As @johnfoliot notes, it would be unfortunate if the support for a multilingual Web matching the multilingual world we live in got even worse in browsers, which would be the outcome of just removing this.

Hi Chaals,

You write:

> the value is a machine-readable one

Why? Why is this an @autocomplete *value *that must be machine-readable?
None of the other fields/values are like that*, because the machine -
your user-agent - doesn't need to read anything more than "this field
expects a value corresponding to this concept" (*the token value*), which
is what autocomplete does.

I believe the "machine-readable" part is being mis-understood: the machine
reads the token value and then acts upon that, by echoing back a stored
value: the user-response is simply the string of data the user has stored
on their machine - the field is then populated with that random string,
because the machine read the unambiguous token value.

Forcing authors to capture responses in a specific format is overly
restrictive: why should I, as a form author, use an ISO language code value
to submit *an answer* to **my database**? Why is the spec mandating I must
capture the answer in a specific format? What does the standard know about
my form's needs? (Answer: nothing)

[* I am actually incorrect here: in a similar but different example, the
token for "country" is demanding a **Valid ISO 3166-1-alpha-2 country code**
<https://www.iso.org/iso-3166-country-codes.html>, but (I suspect) because
some forms may want to capture a full text string instead, there is also "country-name" 
which takes **Free-form text, no newlines** for, I will argue,
exactly the same reason: not all form owners need or want the ISO Country
value, a text string response is sufficient.

<input type="text' name="country" value="ประเทศไทย">

If the spec MUST maintain a token that demands a specific format string
from *the response* ('language'), then we likely need a companion token
value "language-name" that can accept **Free-form text, no newlines** - ya?]

JF
